headline: Sustained collaboration with private sector essential for building competitive economy, says finance minister
description: ISLAMABAD - Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb Monday met with Ali Hussam Asghar, president of the Lahore Chamber of Commerce
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb Monday met with Ali Hussam Asghar, president of the Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI), to discuss measures for promoting sustainable, export-led economic growth, supporting small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and improving the overall business environment.

The finance minister welcomed Ali Hussam Asghar and highlighted the government’s commitment to achieving sustainable economic growth through greater private-sector participation, enhanced competitiveness and an expanded export base. He emphasised that exports must remain central to the country’s growth strategy and that policies should facilitate exporters in becoming more competitive in regional and int’l markets.

The finance minister highlighted that improving the ease of doing business requires a facilitative and predictable policy environment, simplified regulatory processes and effective coordination among relevant institutions. He underscored the importance of addressing the concerns of businesses, particularly SMEs, and ensuring that government policies support investment, productivity, employment generation and business expansion.

Ali Hussam Asghar shared the LCCI’s perspective on promoting SMEs, improving access to finance and facilitating business expansion. He emphasised the importance of a supportive business ecosystem, greater policy predictability, modernisation and export growth. He also highlighted the importance of continued consultation with chambers of commerce and industry to ensure that business policies address ground-level challenges and support sustainable economic activity. The discussion also covered ways to strengthen the SME sector as an important driver of economic activity, exports and employment. The finance minister highlighted the importance of improving access to finance, facilitating business expansion and encouraging investment in modernisation and capacity-building. He also emphasised the practical and targeted measures to encourage businesses to expand their operations, increase investment and contribute to economic growth. The finance minister observed that taxation and regulatory policies should support productive economic activity while promoting documentation and broadening the tax base. He emphasised the value of evidence-based policymaking and constructive engagement with the business community to assess the impact of proposed measures on businesses, investment and employment. He also underlined the importance of simplifying procedures and building greater confidence between businesses and government institutions.

Emphasising the importance of policy continuity and predictability, Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb highlighted the role of the Tax Policy Office in maintaining sustained engagement with the private sector and developing a medium-term tax policy framework. He noted that a stable and predictable policy environment would enable businesses to make informed investment decisions and plan for long-term growth.

The finance minister reaffirmed the government’s commitment to working closely with chambers of commerce, industry representatives and other stakeholders to address business-related matters, promote SMEs and facilitate exporters. He observed that sustained collaboration with the private sector is essential to building a competitive economy driven by investment, productivity and exports. The meeting was also attended by Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kiyani, Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan, Federal Secretary Finance, and senior representatives from the Tax Policy Office, Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and Finance Division.

headline: Ambassador Syed Haider Shah assumes charge as Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to UN
description: Mateen Haider googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display('div-gpt-ad-1681982472501-0'); }); ISLAMABADPakistan’s newly appointed
author: MATEEN HAIDER
article_text:
Mateen Haider

ISLAMABAD Pakistan’s newly appointed Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, has formally assumed his responsibilities at Pakistan’s Permanent Mission in New York, marking the beginning of his diplomatic assignment at a critical time for Pakistan’s engagement with the United Nations and the international community.

“Yes, I have joined my new responsibilities as Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations,” Ambassador Shah confirmed to The Nation over the phone on Monday.

Ambassador Shah was appointed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to the prestigious diplomatic position in October on the recommendations of Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad as part of a series of key diplomatic postings and reshuffles in Pakistan’s Foreign Service. Prior to his appointment, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah was serving as Pakistan’s Ambassador to the Netherlands, based in The Hague, where he represented Pakistan’s diplomatic interests and pursued bilateral engagement with the European country. His appointment as Pakistan’s top diplomat at the United Nations comes at an important juncture, as Islamabad continues to pursue its diplomatic priorities at the global forum, including regional peace and security, the Kashmir dispute, multilateral cooperation and the protection of Pakistan’s national interests. The Permanent Representative to the United Nations is Pakistan’s principal diplomatic representative at the UN headquarters in New York and plays a central role in coordinating the country’s engagement with the UN Security Council, General Assembly and other multilateral bodies.

Ambassador Syed Haider Shah has three decades of experience in diplomacy, particularly in multilateral diplomacy. At the headquarters of the Foreign Office, he served as additional secretary United Nations desk.

Earlier, he served in Nepal as Pakistan Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires of Pakistan in New Delhi.

The Permanent Representative to the United Nations is Pakistan’s principal diplomatic representative at the UN headquarters in New York and plays a central role in coordinating the country’s engagement with the UN Security Council, General Assembly and other multilateral bodies.

Ambassador Syed Haider Shah has three decades of experience in diplomacy, particularly in multilateral diplomacy. At the headquarters of the Foreign Office, he served as additional secretary United Nations desk.
Earlier, he served in Nepal as Pakistan Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires of Pakistan in New Delhi.

headline: Houthis say they launched drones at Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport
description: SANAA/RIYADH - Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched drones towards Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport as well as an
author: News Desk
article_text:
SANAA/RIYADH - Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched drones towards Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport as well as an early-warning radar in Jizan and a military transport aircraft at Jizan airport. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.

Early warning alerts were issued across several parts of Saudi Arabia on Monday morning over potential security threats, while air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward the southern region. The first alert was issued through the Early Warning Platform at 8:58 a.m. for Khamis Mushait Governorate, followed shortly by alerts in Taif, Abha and Najran. Around noon, another alert was issued for Jazan Region, followed by a second alert for Najran in the afternoon. The all-clear was subsequently issued for the affected areas, indicating that the threats had passed. According to an announcement by the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi militia toward the Kingdom’s southern region. In its early warning notifications, the Saudi Civil Defense urged residents who received alerts to follow official safety instructions and contact 988 in the event of an emergency.

headline: Inflation drops to 9.6pc in October, within govt projection
description: ISLAMABAD - Pakistan’s inflation rate was recorded at 9.6 percent in October this year over the same period of the last year. The monthly inflation
author: Imran Ali Kundi
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Pakistan’s inflation rate was recorded at 9.6 percent in October this year over the same period of the last year. The monthly inflation rate, measured through Consumer Price Indicator (CPI), was recorded at 9.6 percent in October this year, according to the latest data of Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS). The inflation rate was 10.3 percent in September after touching 11.1 percent in August this year. On a month-on-month basis, it increased by 1.1 percent in October 2026 as compared to an increase of 1.3 percent in the previous month and an increase of 1.7 percent in October 2025.

The CPI inflation urban remained at 9.5 percent on a year-on-year basis in the last month. Meanwhile, the CPI inflation for rural areas increased by 9.8 percent in October 2026. Inflation measured by Sensitive Price Index (SPI) increased by 9.62 percent and Wholesale Price Indicator (WPI) based inflation enhanced by 12.1 percent. The inflation rate remained within the projection of the government. “Headline inflation is projected in the range of 9.5 to 10.5 percent for October 2026, with the subsequent path sensitive to international energy prices, food supplies and base effects.,” the Ministry of Finance had said in its Monthly Economic Update & Outlook (September 2026).

The break-up of inflation of 9.6 percent showed that food and non-alcoholic beverages prices increased by 7.74 percent last month. Similarly, health and education charges went up by 8.09 percent and 8.03 percent, respectively. Similarly, prices of utilities (housing, water, electricity, gas and fuel) increased by 11.03 percent in the last month. Meanwhile, the prices of alcoholic beverages and tobacco went up by around 3.16 percent. Prices of clothing and footwear increased by 9.19 percent and furnishing and household equipment maintenance charges 7.19 percent. Recreational charges and those related to culture went up by 1.73 percent in the period under review, while amounts charged by restaurants and hotels by 6 percent in October 2026 as compared to the same month last year.

In rural areas, the food items which saw their prices increased included fresh vegetables (19.59 percent), chicken (16.91 percent), fresh fruits (9.43 percent), wheat flour (9.41 percent), wheat (9 percent), pulse gram (8.3 percent), besan (5.51 percent), eggs (5.08 percent), wheat products (3.74 percent), pulse mash (3.34 percent), gram whole (2.74 percent), pulse masoor (2.25 percent), dry fruits (1.41 percent) and pulse moong (1.34 percent).

In non-food commodities, prices of following items enhanced: postal services (33.33 percent), liquified hydrocarbons (4.41 percent), motor fuels (3.17 percent), solid fuel (2 percent), footwear (1.80 percent), construction input items (1.53 percent), drugs and medicines (1.38 percent), medical tests (1.33 percent), garbage collection (1.22 percent), hospitals services (1.17 percent) and household textiles (1.14 percent). In rural areas, prices of the following items decreased: tomatoes (29.63 percent), potatoes (9.25 percent), onions (6.51 percent), gur (2.02 percent), sugar (1.32 percent) and rice (0.03 percent).

In urban areas, prices of following commodities increased: chicken (19.38 percent), pulse gram (9.17 percent), wheat (9.01 percent), wheat flour (7.54 percent), fresh vegetables (6.55 percent), eggs (5.72 percent), besan (5.54 percent), gram whole (4.19 percent), fresh fruits (2.70 percent), wheat products (2.27 percent), pulse mash (2.16 percent), fish (1.42 percent), dry fruits (1.37 percent) and pulse masoor (1.29 percent).

headline: Govt replacing red tape with red carpet for investors, Bangladeshi minister told
description: ISLAMABAD - Advisor to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan Monday received Bangladesh’s Minister for Finance and
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Advisor to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan Monday received Bangladesh’s Minister for Finance and Planning, Rashid Al Mahmud Titumir, along with his delegation, to discuss bilateral relations, industrial cooperation, export-led growth and opportunities for strengthening economic ties between the two countries. The meeting was attended by Rana Ihsan Afzal, Coordinator to the Prime Minister on Industries and Commerce, Humaira Zia Mufti, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Industries and Production, and Freedoon Akram Sheikh, Joint Secretary.

Welcoming the visiting minister and his delegation, Haroon Akhtar Khan said that Pakistan and Bangladesh shared brotherly relations rooted in common cultural heritage and historical connections. On behalf of the people of Pakistan, he warmly welcomed the distinguished guests and expressed his desire to further strengthen bilateral engagement. The advisor said that Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif attached particular importance to strengthening relations with regional countries and promoting economic cooperation through mutually beneficial partnerships.

Highlighting Pakistan’s ongoing industrial transformation, Haroon Akhtar Khan said the government was introducing regulatory reforms to facilitate investment, accelerate industrial development and improve the business environment. He emphasized that the government’s approach was to replace red tape with a red carpet for investors, ensuring greater facilitation and ease of doing business. The advisor also stressed the importance of export-led growth, manufacturing expansion, industrial productivity and value addition as key pillars for strengthening economic cooperation between the two countries.

During the meeting, Bangladesh’s Minister for Finance and Planning Rashid Al Mahmud Titumir expressed warm sentiments towards Pakistan and its people, describing the relationship between the two countries as brotherly. The visiting minister shared Bangladesh’s economic experience and highlighted the country’s progress in overcoming various economic challenges. He stated that Bangladesh had made significant efforts to stabilize its microeconomic and macroeconomic indicators while achieving improvements in industrial growth and manufacturing. He also emphasized the potential for expanding economic and industrial cooperation between Pakistan and Bangladesh, noting that stronger bilateral engagement could create new opportunities for both countries. headline: Fiscal surplus narrows to 0.8pc of GDP in first quarter
description: ISLAMABAD - Pakistan’s overall fiscal surplus narrowed to 0.8 percent of GDP (Rs1,197.9 billion) in the first quarter of the current fiscal year
author: Imran Ali Kundi
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Pakistan’s overall fiscal surplus narrowed to 0.8 percent of GDP (Rs1,197.9 billion) in the first quarter of the current fiscal year (2026-27) compared with 1.7 percent of GDP (Rs2,123.8 billion) in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.

Net federal revenue amounted to Rs2,912.9 billion, exceeding federal expenditure of Rs2,124.4 billion and contributing to a federal fiscal surplus equivalent to 0.5 percent of GDP. FBR tax collection registered a growth of 3.6 percent during the period. Total expenditure increased by 20.7 percent, driven primarily by a 69.5 percent surge in development expenditure, significantly outpacing the 14.7 percent growth in current expenditure. The relatively moderate increase in current expenditure was largely attributable to an 8.1 percent decline in non-interest expenditure, mainly reflecting a sharp 90.0 percent reduction in subsidies. In contrast, mark-up payments increased by 36.6 percent.

“Fiscal operations began FY2027 on a positive note, with both the overall and primary fiscal balances recording surpluses during July-August”, the ministry of finance stated in its recent report. The primary surplus declined to 1.6 percent of GDP (Rs 2,311.2 billion), from 2.3 percent of GDP (Rs 2,938.9 billion) recorded in the same period last year. During Jul-Sep FY2027, FBR tax collection grew by 7.0 percent to reach Rs3,086.2 billion, exceeding the target by Rs33.2 billion. Both direct and indirect taxes posted positive growth, increasing by 5.5 percent and 8.3 percent, respectively. Within indirect taxes, sales tax recorded the strongest growth at 11.6 percent, followed by federal excise duty at 3.6 percent and customs duties at 0.5 percent. The fiscal deficit target for Pakistan’s federal budget 2026–27 is 3.6% of GDP, paired with a primary surplus target of 2.0% of GDP.

However, the government would have to depend on tax collection of the FBR to maintain the budget deficit within the target. The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) had collected Rs4.089 trillion during the first four months (July-October) of the current fiscal year (FY27), falling short of its target of Rs4.185 trillion by Rs96 billion. Overall revenue collection posted modest growth of 6 per cent compared to Rs3.840 trillion collected during the same period last year.

headline: Adrian Hamilton-Manns takes charge as PIA CEO
description: Islamabad - Pakistan International Airlines’ Board is pleased to announce the appointment of Mr Adrian Hamilton-Manns as the Chief Executive Officer of
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Islamabad - Pakistan International Airlines’ Board is pleased to announce the appointment of Mr Adrian Hamilton-Manns as the Chief Executive Officer of the national carrier. According to a statement, he has assumed charge of the office from Monday.

Mr Hamilton-Manns brings a wealth of leadership and strategic experience within the global aviation sector. His appointment marks a pivotal chapter in PIA’s ongoing transformation. He has to his credit managing three airlines as a CEO, and is considered a world expert in transformation and reviving airlines. His professional experience spans over 30 years. As Mr Hamilton-Manns assumes the role of CEO, the consortium and the entire management board extend their deepest gratitude to the outgoing Chief Executive Officer, Air Vice Marshal (AVM) Amir Hayat, for his outstanding service and dedication to this vital national role. Over his four-and-a-half-year tenure, AVM Amir Hayat’s decisive leadership was instrumental in navigating the airline through significant industry challenges. His relentless efforts were central to initiating comprehensive structural reforms, optimizing operational efficiencies, and successfully preparing the airline for its highly anticipated privatization phase. The foundation he has laid will be critical to the carrier’s future commercial viability and success. “We are immensely grateful for AVM Amir Hayat’s steadfast commitment to the national flag carrier during a highly complex transitional period,” Chairman of the PIA Board stated.

“As we welcome Mr. Adrian to the helm, we are confident that his extensive industry expertise will accelerate our strategic objectives, elevate our service standards, and drive sustainable profitability in this new era for PIA.”

As Mr Hamilton-Manns assumes the role of CEO, the consortium and the entire management board extend their deepest gratitude to the outgoing Chief Executive Officer, Air Vice Marshal (AVM) Amir Hayat, for his outstanding service and dedication to this vital national role. Over his four-and-a-half-year tenure, AVM Amir Hayat’s decisive leadership was instrumental in navigating the airline through significant industry challenges. His relentless efforts were central to initiating comprehensive structural reforms, optimizing operational efficiencies, and successfully preparing the airline for its highly anticipated privatization phase. The foundation he has laid will be critical to the carrier’s future commercial viability and success. “We are immensely grateful for AVM Amir Hayat’s steadfast commitment to the national flag carrier during a highly complex transitional period,” Chairman of the PIA Board stated.

“As we welcome Mr. Adrian to the helm, we are confident that his extensive industry expertise will accelerate our strategic objectives, elevate our service standards, and drive sustainable profitability in this new era for PIA.”

headline: CM Maryam gives officials 15 days to ensure province-wide cleanliness
description: LAHORE - Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif on Monday gave the authorities a 15-day deadline to bring about a 100 per cent improvement in cleanliness
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
LAHORE - Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif on Monday gave the authorities a 15-day deadline to bring about a 100 per cent improvement in cleanliness across the province, expressing dissatisfaction with the performance of solid waste management companies.

Chairing a special meeting to review the Suthra Punjab programme, the chief minister decided in principle to terminate the services of waste management companies over unsatisfactory cleanliness arrangements. The meeting also approved a shift to self-operation of sanitation services in Lahore, Faisalabad, Gujranwala, Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan. Expressing concern over dust and dirt on roads across the province, Maryam Nawaz directed the authorities to ensure daily washing of main roads. She also ordered fines for people found littering roads after cleaning operations and directed strict action against those dumping garbage in markets, bazaars, vegetable, fruit and grain markets. The meeting set targets for ensuring adequate human resources and machinery in every district, while the chief minister directed that villages be cleaned on alternate days.

She instructed deputy commissioners and assistant commissioners to hold weekly meetings with Field Monitoring Officers (FMOs) and directed the formulation of key performance indicators (KPIs) to evaluate their performance. The chief minister also ordered timely payment of salaries to sanitation workers in every city and locality, emphasising that workers should not face delays in receiving their wages. She sought details from all deputy commissioners about the machinery required for sanitation operations, along with a comprehensive record of savings expected through the self-operation model.

The meeting also discussed imposing fines on owners of vacant plots where garbage was found dumped.

Deputy commissioners of Multan, Rajanpur, Dera Ghazi Khan, Hafizabad, Muzaffargarh and other districts presented reports on cleanliness arrangements in their respective areas.

Maryam Nawaz directed all deputy commissioners to physically verify the availability and condition of machinery and equipment in their districts. She also convened a follow-up meeting on the Suthra Punjab programme after one week to review progress.

headline: Police constable injured in Peshawar firing; blast damages vehicle in Bannu
description: PESHAWAR - A police constable was injured here on Monday when unidentified armed men opened fire in the Bhana Mari area. The injured official was shifted to a
author: NEWS WIRE
article_text: PESHAWAR - A police constable was injured here on Monday when unidentified armed men opened fire in the Bhana Mari area. The injured official was shifted to a hospital for medical treatment, while the attackers escaped after the shooting. Police launched a search operation in the area to trace and arrest the suspects. In a separate incident in Bannu, an explosion near a police vehicle close to City Miryan Gate damaged the vehicle, while the personnel remained unharmed. According to sources, the police vehicle was on routine patrol when an improvised explosive device (IED) planted in the area exploded.

headline: YFK delegation briefed on Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts for Kashmir
description: ISLAMABAD - A 40-member delegation of the Youth Forum for Kashmir (YFK), led by its Executive Director Zaman Bajwa, visited the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
author: SHAFQAT ALI
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - A 40-member delegation of the Youth Forum for Kashmir (YFK), led by its Executive Director Zaman Bajwa, visited the Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday and received a briefing on Pakistan’s foreign policy priorities, particularly its diplomatic efforts to highlight the Jammu and Kashmir dispute at international forums.

The delegation was received by Foreign Office spokesperson Ambassador Sajjad Haider Khan, who outlined Pakistan’s principal foreign policy objectives and reaffirmed the country’s unwavering commitment to the legitimate rights and aspirations of the Kashmiri people. During the briefing, the spokesperson highlighted Pakistan’s sustained diplomatic engagement to draw international attention to the Jammu and Kashmir dispute, reiterating Islamabad’s consistent position that its just, peaceful and lasting resolution must be achieved in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions.

He underscored Pakistan’s principled stance on the dispute and its continued efforts to advocate for the rights of the Kashmiri people through diplomatic channels and international platforms. The briefing was followed by an interactive question-and-answer session, during which members of the delegation engaged in a substantive exchange of views on Pakistan’s foreign policy, diplomatic priorities and the role of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in safeguarding and advancing the country’s national interests. The visit provided the young participants with an opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of Pakistan’s diplomatic engagements, foreign policy objectives and its continued commitment to supporting the Kashmiri people’s legitimate aspirations, the FO said. The interaction also highlighted the importance of engaging youth in understanding Pakistan’s foreign policy and diplomatic efforts on key national and international issues.

headline: Pak, China reaffirm commitment to strengthen all-weather strategic partnership
description: ISLAMABAD - Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China
author: SHAFQAT ALI
article_text: ISLAMABAD - Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, yesterday reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening Pakistan-China relations and maintaining close coordination to sustain the positive momentum in bilateral ties. During a bilateral meeting here, the two leaders discussed ways to enhance cultural cooperation and promote people-to-people exchanges, underscoring the importance of deepening the longstanding friendship between the two countries. Minister Liu conveyed greetings from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, which Ishaq Dar warmly reciprocated. The DPM also conveyed warm greetings to Chinese President Xi Jinping on behalf of Pakistan’s leadership. Ishaq Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s unwavering commitment to further strengthening the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership with China, highlighting the importance Islamabad attaches to its enduring relationship with Beijing. Both sides expressed their resolve to maintain close coordination and build on the positive momentum in bilateral relations, reaffirming their shared commitment to advancing cooperation and further consolidating the Pakistan-China friendship, the Foreign Office said. The meeting reflected the continued high-level engagement between Pakistan and China and their determination to strengthen bilateral ties through enhanced cooperation, cultural exchanges and closer institutional coordination.

description: QUETTA - The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly held under the Chair of Asghar Ali Tareen, the committee addressed major
author: NEWS WIRE
article_text:
QUETTA - The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly held under the Chair of Asghar Ali Tareen, the committee addressed major financial irregularities, audit objections, and accountability lapses across provincial departments, highlighting a massive accounting discrepancy of over seven billion rupees in provincial accounts as well as significant financial default at a premier provincial university.

The meeting was attended by committee members Rahmat Saleh Baloch, Wali Muhammad Noorzai, and Zabid Ali Reki, alongside senior provincial leadership including Secretary Assembly Tahir Shah Kakar, Accountant General Nasrullah Jan, Director General Audit Shuja Ali, Secretary Finance Muhammad Jahangir Khan Kakar, Special Secretary PAC Siraj Lehri, and Additional Secretary Law Saeed Iqbal. During the opening session, the committee evaluated the Certification Audit Report of the Accountant General of Balochistan. Proceedings began with sharp criticism from the chair and committee members over the initial absence of the Finance Secretary.

Committee member Rahmat Saleh Baloch stressed that the presence of top financial officials is mandatory during certification audits to ensure direct accountability and effective progress. Finance Secretary Muhammad Jahangir Khan Kakar subsequently joined the meeting to brief the panel. The committee expressed grave concern over severe discrepancies between physical cash figures, ledger books, and bank records. Audit findings revealed that as of June 30, 2023, financial statements reflected an account balance exceeding 23.06 billion rupees, whereas State Bank of Pakistan records showed approximately 15.29 billion rupees, leaving an un-reconciled gap of nearly 7.71 billion rupees. Audit officials attributed this variance to poor record-keeping, failure to post un-cashed cheques, and a persistent lack of timely reconciliation between the Finance Department, the State Bank of Pakistan, and the National Bank of Pakistan.

headline: US child-safety alert leads NCCIA to child abuse network
description: ISLAMABAD - An international child-safety alert has led Pakistan’s National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to arrest two men suspected of
author: Haris Shirazi
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - An international child-safety alert has led Pakistan’s National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to arrest two men suspected of involvement in a network allegedly involved in recording, sharing and circulating videos of the sexual abuse of young children, including those as young as one year old.

The investigation began after a social media platform detected suspected child sexual abuse material and reported it to the US-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). The information was subsequently referred to the relevant authorities in Pakistan, prompting an NCCIA investigation that led to the arrest of the first suspect and, later, a second accused. An Islamabad court has granted four days’ further physical remand of each suspect, while investigators are continuing efforts to trace other individuals allegedly involved in the network. Officials familiar with the investigation told The Nation that the case originated from an NCMEC report generated following the detection of suspected child abuse material online.

The centre works with technology companies, including Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and Google, which report suspected child exploitation content through established reporting mechanisms. Such reports may contain relevant account information and technical details, including IP addresses, which can assist law-enforcement agencies in identifying suspects. The officials said that cases involving the sexual exploitation of very young children were particularly disturbing, with victims in the cases under investigation often aged five or younger, including children between one and four years of age.

Acting on the information received, the NCCIA arrested the first suspect, identified as Sajid Ali, a resident of Skardu, on October 26. According to the officials, investigators recovered suspected child sexual abuse material from his mobile phones, including footage allegedly involving children in Pakistan as well as material originating from other countries.

His interrogation subsequently led investigators to a second suspect, who was arrested on October 29. The officials alleged that the second accused had recorded videos of the sexual abuse of his own very young child and shared them with Sajid. They further alleged that Sajid had paid Rs7,000 for one such video. During interrogation, the second suspect reportedly told investigators that he had recorded the footage at Sajid’s request and in return for money.

Investigators also found that Sajid was allegedly active in Telegram groups used to circulate child sexual abuse material. According to the officials, he contacted members of these groups, claimed to possess additional videos and encouraged others to share similar material. During interrogation, Sajid reportedly told investigators that his involvement was motivated by what he described as “mental satisfaction”, the officials said. Although investigators have not established a financial motive beyond the alleged payment of Rs7,000, they have sought bank statements to examine possible transactions linked to the suspects.

Officials said that if evidence of international payments or other financial dealings emerged, the individuals receiving or making such payments would also be questioned. The first information report (FIR) was registered on October 26 at the NCCIA’s Cyber Crime Reporting Centre in Islamabad following a preliminary inquiry. The case has been registered under relevant provisions of the cybercrime law and the Pakistan Penal Code. Investigating Officer Muhammad Waseem Khan, a sub-inspector, had sought eight days’ further physical remand of both suspects before the Judicial Magistrate (West), arguing that additional interrogation was necessary to establish the extent of their involvement and identify other members of the alleged network. According to the investigating officer, Sajid had previously remained on six days’ physical remand, while the second suspect had been remanded for three days.

He told the court that investigators needed to examine their electronic devices and social media accounts in their presence and trace other suspected accomplices on the basis of information provided by the accused. The court granted four days’ further physical remand of each suspect and directed the investigating agency to produce them again on November 6. Officials said NCMEC referrals had become an important source of information for Pakistan’s cybercrime investigators dealing with online child exploitation. However, scale and frequency of such referrals, as well as proportion of investigations initiated through them, could not be independently established from the information available.

He told the court that investigators needed to examine their electronic devices and social media accounts in their presence and trace other suspected accomplices on the basis of information provided by the accused. The court granted four days’ further physical remand of each suspect and directed the investigating agency to produce them again on November 6. Officials said NCMEC referrals had become an important source of information for Pakistan’s cybercrime investigators dealing with online child exploitation. However, scale and frequency of such referrals, as well as proportion of investigations initiated through them, could not be independently established from the information available.

headline: Past in Perspective
description: The Gulf War, fought from 1990 to 1991, stemmed from Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, prompting international condemnation and military intervention led by a
author: The Nation
article_text: The Gulf War, fought from 1990 to 1991, stemmed from Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, prompting international condemnation and military intervention led by a coalition of nations, primarily the United States. This conflict marked a turning point in modern warfare, showcasing the effectiveness of precision airstrikes and coalition-based military operations. Its significance lies in reshaping geopolitics in the Middle East, leading to increased U.S. military presence in the region and setting the stage for subsequent conflicts and instability. The Gulf War also highlighted the importance of international alliances and diplomacy in addressing regional security threats, echoing in ongoing tensions and interventions in the region today.

headline: AI’s Future
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the global job market and changing how people work. While technological progress creates new opportunities, it
author: The Nation
article_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the global job market and changing how people work. While technological progress creates new opportunities, it also presents challenges, making it essential to prepare young people for the future.

AI is increasingly used in education, healthcare, business and software development to analyse information, automate routine tasks and improve productivity. However, its growing adoption has raised concerns about job security, particularly for workers performing repetitive tasks.

As technology advances, skills such as digital literacy, critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving will become increasingly important. Some existing jobs may also change or disappear, making retraining and lifelong learning essential.

In Pakistan, many young people lack access to quality digital education and practical technical training. Without proper preparation, they may struggle to compete in an increasingly technology-driven job market.

The government should modernise educational curricula and introduce practical courses in programming, data analysis, and the responsible use of AI. Educational institutions should collaborate with employers to provide relevant training, while affordable internet access and scholarships can help students from low-income families.

Young people should not view AI solely as a threat. Instead, they should learn to use it responsibly while developing human skills such as empathy, leadership, judgement, and communication.

AI can contribute to economic and social progress if its benefits are shared fairly. The relevant authorities must take timely steps to equip young people with the knowledge and skills needed to succeed in the future job market.

ANAAB HAJI SABZAL,

Absor.

headline: Value of Leaving Things Unfinished
description: We live in a world where everyone wants to finish everything on time. We make plans, set goals, and try to complete every task. Yet, in our busy lives, we
author: The Nation
article_text:
We live in a world where everyone wants to finish everything on time. We make plans, set goals, and try to complete every task. Yet, in our busy lives, we often forget that not everything needs to be finished.

Sometimes, we continue with things simply because we have already started them. We remain in situations that make us unhappy, follow plans that no longer suit us, and spend time explaining ourselves to people who refuse to understand. We often mistake stopping for failure.

But is stopping always a failure?

Leaving something unfinished can sometimes be a wise decision. A student may change career plans after discovering a new interest, while someone may stop trying to please everyone and begin recognising their own needs. Such choices do not necessarily mean giving up; they can be signs of learning and growth.

We are taught to celebrate success, but rarely discuss the importance of knowing when to move on. Not every plan works out, and not every question has an answer. Sometimes, we need time to understand what is right for us.

This does not mean avoiding responsibilities or abandoning everything halfway. It means learning to distinguish between giving up too soon and moving on for a good reason.

Life is not a list of tasks that must be completed perfectly. Some experiences are valuable because of what they teach us, even when they do not end as expected.

Perhaps growing up is not just about learning to finish things, but also about recognising when it is time to move on.

JAVERIA ABID,

Karachi.

headline: Opening New Vistas
description: E-commerce has emerged as a promising avenue for Pakistan’s digital economy, creating opportunities for enterprise, employment and trade among its young
author: The Nation
article_text:
E-commerce has emerged as a promising avenue for Pakistan’s digital economy, creating opportunities for enterprise, employment and trade among its young and increasingly connected population. The spread of smartphones, internet access and digital payments has transformed the marketplace, allowing small businesses, home-based entrepreneurs, artisans and students to reach customers nationwide without investing in physical outlets.

The sector’s growth is reflected in online transactions, which increased by 195 per cent between 2020 and 2024, while their total value rose by 402 per cent to Rs218.1 billion in 2024. Digital channels accounted for approximately 88 per cent of retail payment transactions by volume in FY2025. These figures highlight changing consumer behaviour and the considerable potential for further growth.

Pakistan’s young population can turn this transformation into an economic advantage. Students can establish online businesses, artisans can access national markets, and small manufacturers can reach international customers through digital platforms.

However, this potential cannot be realised through taxation alone. Excessive duties, complicated regulations, expensive logistics and inadequate digital infrastructure can discourage businesses and increase costs. The government should adopt a facilitative approach by introducing a predictable tax regime, strengthening digital payment systems, improving internet infrastructure and helping small and medium-sized enterprises establish an online presence.

Foreign platforms should also be welcomed for the competition, technology and market access they offer, provided they operate under fair and transparent regulations that protect local businesses from unfair competition.

More importantly, e-commerce should be recognised not merely as a convenient way to buy and sell goods, but as an export channel through which Pakistani products can reach global markets. With appropriate policies, digital skills and reliable infrastructure, Pakistan can create livelihoods, bring small businesses into the formal economy and generate valuable foreign exchange.

The digital marketplace is already here. Pakistan now needs the vision and consistent policies to ensure that its people do not merely participate in this transformation but benefit from its vast economic potential.

RANA MUHAMMAD FAZEEL DASTGIR,

Lahore.

Excessive duties, complicated regulations, expensive logistics and inadequate digital infrastructure can discourage businesses and increase costs. The government should adopt a facilitative approach by introducing a predictable tax regime, strengthening digital payment systems, improving internet infrastructure and helping small and medium-sized enterprises

establish an online presence.

Foreign platforms should also be welcomed for the competition, technology and market access they offer, provided they operate under fair and transparent regulations that protect local businesses from unfair competition.

More importantly, e-commerce should be recognised not merely as a convenient way to buy and sell goods, but as an export channel through which Pakistani products can reach global markets. With appropriate policies, digital skills and reliable infrastructure, Pakistan can create livelihoods, bring small businesses into the formal economy and generate valuable foreign exchange.

The digital marketplace is already here. Pakistan now needs the vision and consistent policies to ensure that its people do not merely participate in this transformation but benefit from its vast economic potential.
RANA MUHAMMAD FAZEEL DASTGIR,
Lahore.

headline: Geopolitics of AI Empires
description: Everyone is hunting chokepoints now. Washington warns allies against depending on China while looking for ways to exploit their dependence on the American
author: Manzoor Malik
article_text:
Everyone is hunting chokepoints now. Washington warns allies against depending on China while looking for ways to exploit their dependence on the American market, technology and dollar. Beijing answers with rare earths. Iran eyes the Strait of Hormuz. A recent Foreign Affairs essay by Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman and Yeling Tan calls the result a chokepoint trap: each state’s effort to make itself safer makes others feel less safe, and since restraint invites victimhood, the likeliest outcome is a fragmented, volatile world.

Artificial intelligence is the biggest chokepoint stack ever built. Niall Ferguson, Lisa Klaassen and Eric Schmidt argue that America and China have become AI empires, with dominion over the models, chips, minerals and capital everyone else needs. Pax Silica, the US-led coalition on chips and critical minerals, was launched last December, and India joined in February.

Countries like Pakistan are often seen as ‘takers’ in the global order. While this may be true in an economic sense, it is an inaccurate description of the state itself. Empires depend on scarce inputs and demand allegiance, yet Pakistan holds more cards than it plays. Strategically, it is uniquely positioned at the crossroads of South Asia, the Gulf, Central Asia and China. As a nuclear-armed state, it has also secured mutual defence agreements with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. Furthermore, its resource potential is growing; the first mineral shipment under a US memorandum moved in October 2025, alongside its vast hydropower capabilities and a young, dynamic market. Finally, Pakistan maintains a strong diplomatic record, having argued for years that machines should not decide who lives or dies.

It remains to be seen how Pakistan plays the situation. Data Vault Pakistan runs a sovereign cloud on about 3,000 Nvidia GPUs obtained through US-approved channels, while Gul Ahmed Energy Group is building a Huawei data centre worth up to USD 600 million. One track is American, the other Chinese, and nobody has said whether this is a strategy or an accident. Pakistan spends an estimated USD 700 to 800 million a year on foreign computing resources and negotiates each deal separately, like a buyer. That is the behaviour gap, and it is a gap of policy, not of position.

In a chokepoint trap, the danger for a mid-sized, dollar-dependent state lies less in being directly targeted than in becoming collateral damage. Because foreign rules are often written ambiguously, banks, vendors and cloud providers tend to over-comply, leaving the end user to bear the costs. Therefore, Pakistan needs a dedicated sanctions and export-control interpretation unit, a robust compliance firewall between American and Chinese systems, and a clear-headed review of its leverage. A true chokepoint requires a near-monopoly with no easy substitutes; consequently, Pakistan’s minerals and geography should be viewed as bargaining chips to secure refining capabilities and technical skills, not as strategic weapons.

Wall Street is nervous. Oracle had its worst week since the dot-com bust in June, down 19 per cent in five days, and the five largest US companies are worth about USD 18 trillion while borrowing to fund AI. The labour market is moving before any crash: Barclays has cut around 5,000 jobs in an efficiency drive and is reportedly using AI and offshoring to India to deliver a GBP 2 billion savings plan. For Pakistan, that cuts both ways, since the tools that make offshoring cheaper can also replace the offshored roles. Add Washington’s H-1B crackdown, which has cut new approvals from nearly 140,000 in 2024 to around 52,000, and a year in which entry-level hiring at major Pakistani tech firms fell by a quarter even as IT exports hit USD 4.6 billion. A state needs a corporate IT base, not just gig income.

Yet the trap is not destiny. In their new Foreign Affairs essay, ‘AI Is a Choice’, Alex Imas, Mohamed El-Erian and James Manyika argue that AI is a cooperative game, as the biggest gains arise only when many groups coordinate and last only when each expects to do better inside the coalition than outside. Globalisation’s lesson is that gains spread widely while losses concentrate, causing public trust to collapse; for instance, 70 per cent of Americans oppose data centres in their own neighbourhoods. The authors also find that access to AI has spread much faster than adoption, with only about a fifth of tasks in a typical occupation substantially affected so far.

For Pakistan, the bottleneck is domestic, spanning federal and provincial bodies, employers, universities and communities. Each player holds a piece of the puzzle, but nobody is there to coordinate them. Therefore, Pakistan should aim for deep adoption in a few auditable systems, such as tax, procurement and audit. Alongside this, Pakistan should demand community benefit agreements covering power, jobs and skills before any data centre is built, while linking training targets to real employer demand.

The same logic applies abroad. Farrell and his co-authors say escaping the trap requires credible assurances, not just credible threats, and middle powers are well placed to supply them. The Saudi-Pakistan-Türkiye defence pact shows that Pakistan can build binding relationships outside both empires. Along with Gulf partners, Türkiye and others, Pakistan can push for transparency in export-control rules and shared safeguards. In South Asia, where India’s drones and AI-enabled surveillance are rapidly compressing decision times between nuclear-armed neighbours, a published position on human control of AI-enabled weapons would turn Pakistan’s long-standing advocacy for a ban into a doctrine.

None of this works without institutions, because empires operate through local intermediaries who profit from concession terms. We know the pattern from power and procurement: opaque contracts, elite-friendly terms and costs passed on to the public. Independent Power Producers were contracted without a coherent strategy, and citizens are being forced to pay capacity charges for electricity nobody asked for.

Therefore, Pakistan, as a state, needs a concrete agenda. Create a single strategic authority for AI, backed by law and public reporting. Publish sovereignty red lines: military data, national identity systems, and tax and electoral records must never reside on a foreign technology stack. Subject every deal to audit, continuity and exit conditions, with all payments linked to prior and proper scrutiny. Tie every minerals memorandum to refining at home. And watch three tests: whether the authority and red lines exist on paper, how many contracts carry data-residency and exit protections, and whether communities hosting AI infrastructure share in the gains.

The AI race is producing empires at machine speed. Their piling debts, markets and rivalries are making the order unstable. AI is a choice, and so is the order we build around it. It is not a separate policy problem. It is the same problem, wearing a new name.

Manzoor Malik The writer is a public policy professional and CEO of the Governance and Advocacy Foundation for Sustainable Development (GAFSD).

cleaned_blocks.text: Everyone is hunting chokepoints now. Washington warns allies against depending on China while looking for ways to exploit their dependence on the American market, technology and dollar. Beijing answers with rare earths. Iran eyes the Strait of Hormuz. A recent Foreign Affairs essay by Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman and Yeling Tan calls the result a chokepoint trap: each state’s effort to make itself safer makes others feel less safe, and since restraint invites victimhood, the likeliest outcome is a fragmented, volatile world.

Artificial intelligence is the biggest chokepoint stack ever built. Niall Ferguson, Lisa Klaassen and Eric Schmidt argue that America and China have become AI empires, with dominion over the models, chips, minerals and capital everyone else needs. Pax Silica, the US-led coalition on chips and critical minerals, was launched last December, and India joined in February.

Countries like Pakistan are often seen as ‘takers’ in the global order. While this may be true in an economic sense, it is an inaccurate description of the state itself. Empires depend on scarce inputs and demand allegiance, yet Pakistan holds more cards than it plays. Strategically, it is uniquely positioned at the crossroads of South Asia, the Gulf, Central Asia and China. As a nuclear-armed state, it has also secured mutual defence agreements with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. Furthermore, its resource potential is growing; the first mineral shipment under a US memorandum moved in October 2025, alongside its vast hydropower capabilities and a young, dynamic market. Finally, Pakistan maintains a strong diplomatic record, having argued for years that machines should not decide who lives or dies.

It remains to be seen how Pakistan plays the situation. Data Vault Pakistan runs a sovereign cloud on about 3,000 Nvidia GPUs obtained through US-approved channels, while Gul Ahmed Energy Group is building a Huawei data centre worth up to USD 600 million. One track is American, the other Chinese, and nobody has said whether this is a strategy or an accident. Pakistan spends an estimated USD 700 to 800 million a year on foreign computing resources and negotiates each deal separately, like a buyer. That is the behaviour gap, and it is a gap of policy, not of position.

In a chokepoint trap, the danger for a mid-sized, dollar-dependent state lies less in being directly targeted than in becoming collateral damage. Because foreign rules are often written ambiguously, banks, vendors and cloud providers tend to over-comply, leaving the end user to bear the costs. Therefore, Pakistan needs a dedicated sanctions and export-control interpretation unit, a robust compliance firewall between American and Chinese systems, and a clear-headed review of its leverage. A true chokepoint requires a near-monopoly with no easy substitutes; consequently, Pakistan’s minerals and geography should be viewed as bargaining chips to secure refining capabilities and technical skills, not as strategic weapons.

Wall Street is nervous. Oracle had its worst week since the dot-com bust in June, down 19 per cent in five days, and the five largest US companies are worth about USD 18 trillion while borrowing to fund AI. The labour market is moving before any crash: Barclays has cut around 5,000 jobs in an efficiency drive and is reportedly using AI and offshoring to India to deliver a GBP 2 billion savings plan. For Pakistan, that cuts both ways, since the tools that make offshoring cheaper can also replace the offshored roles. Add Washington’s H-1B crackdown, which has cut new approvals from nearly 140,000 in 2024 to around 52,000, and a year in which entry-level hiring at major Pakistani tech firms fell by a quarter even as IT exports hit USD 4.6 billion. A state needs a corporate IT base, not just gig income.

Yet the trap is not destiny. In their new Foreign Affairs essay, ‘AI Is a Choice’, Alex Imas, Mohamed El-Erian and James Manyika argue that AI is a cooperative game, as the biggest gains arise only when many groups coordinate and last only when each expects to do better inside the coalition than outside. Globalisation’s lesson is that gains spread widely while losses concentrate, causing public trust to collapse; for instance, 70 per cent of Americans oppose data centres in their own neighbourhoods. The authors also find that access to AI has spread much faster than adoption, with only about a fifth of tasks in a typical occupation substantially affected so far.

For Pakistan, the bottleneck is domestic, spanning federal and provincial bodies, employers, universities and communities. Each player holds a piece of the puzzle, but nobody is there to coordinate them. Therefore, Pakistan should aim for deep adoption in a few auditable systems, such as tax, procurement and audit. Alongside this, Pakistan should demand community benefit agreements covering power, jobs and skills before any data centre is built, while linking training

targets to real employer demand.

The same logic applies abroad. Farrell and his co-authors say escaping the trap requires credible assurances, not just credible threats, and middle powers are well placed to supply them. The Saudi-Pakistan-Türkiye defence pact shows that Pakistan can build binding relationships outside both empires. Along with Gulf partners, Türkiye and others, Pakistan can push for transparency in export-control rules and shared safeguards. In South Asia, where India’s drones and AI-enabled surveillance are rapidly compressing decision times between nuclear-armed neighbours, a published position on human control of AI-enabled weapons would turn Pakistan’s long-standing advocacy for a ban into a doctrine.

None of this works without institutions, because empires operate through local intermediaries who profit from concession terms. We know the pattern from power and procurement: opaque contracts, elite-friendly terms and costs passed on to the public. Independent Power Producers were contracted without a coherent strategy, and citizens are being forced to pay capacity charges for electricity nobody asked for.

Publish sovereignty red lines: military data, national identity systems, and tax and electoral records must never reside on a foreign technology stack. headline: A Manifesto for National Preparation

author: Syed Ali Shehryar
article_text:
Global powers are restructuring for high-intensity conflict and economic isolation. In the United States (US), defence analysts warn that Washington is preparing for a tactical nuclear strike on Iran. Pentagon orders already require American military bases to operate off-grid for 90 days, while mass purchases of munitions, clothing and boots point to multi-theatre ground wars. Global financial institutions have already priced long-term supply disruptions into global oil and fertiliser forecasts. A US strike on Iran would destabilise Pakistan’s border and lower the nuclear threshold across South Asia and Europe. It would trigger an influx of Baloch separatists and a massive humanitarian refugee crisis. As more troops are pulled towards the western border, India could be tempted to press the eastern front as well. If active hostilities choke the shipping lanes, an economic depression and food crisis could threaten Pakistan’s agricultural backbone.

Other states have already responded to these warnings. European governments have replaced passive civil defence advice with compulsory survival checklists for every household. Canada has ordered its institutions to prepare for total global war under its ‘Plan for a Stronger Canada’. In Pakistan, which is also fighting a multi-front insurgency, the discussion of national readiness is absent.

This systemic unreadiness extends far beyond state policy and is rooted in a crisis of societal resilience. The country’s youth are unprepared to meet the demands an imminent conflict would impose. Mesmerised by superficial displays of strength, Pakistani society has settled into a dangerous passivity, while its affluent classes have retreated into insular luxury. A casual walk through any Pakistani city reveals the rot: convoys of double-cabin trucks clearing the streets, carrying young men flashing weapons for digital clout. A society that mistakes privilege for power cannot absorb a blow from three sides. As history demonstrates, national resolve is forged long before a crisis arrives, built in the homes, schools and civic institutions that stand firm when geopolitical pressure finally hits.

Civil preparedness, therefore, becomes the vital first step. If war shuts the Persian Gulf, Pakistan’s markets will empty and its power grid will come under strain. Pakistan must respond by publishing household readiness guides, training neighbourhood volunteers in first aid and rescue, and issuing rationing guidelines for grain and fuel. At the national level, the time has come to scale up strategic reserves of essential commodities. A prepared citizenry prevents internal chaos, preserving the army’s focus on the front line.

Protecting the home also requires preparing the people inside it through mandatory national service. Pakistan has long maintained a rigid firewall between soldier and civilian, leaving the public to treat national defence as someone else’s responsibility. Compulsory training breaks this divide while formative habits are still taking shape. Finland backs a small peacetime army with male conscription, allowing commanders to mobilise hundreds of thousands of reservists within days, while Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan enforce national service and reserve obligations. Mandatory basic training for students would instil discipline, first-aid skills and a habit of service. A young Pakistani who serves alongside classmates from every class and province learns that the country belongs to all of them.

Training builds the citizen, while a reserve system keeps that citizen on call. A slow, isolated standing army cannot carry an asymmetric war alone, yet Pakistan offers recruits a multi-decade career or nothing. A reserve system would allow graduates who have served three to five years to pause their military careers and return when a crisis erupts, whether war or catastrophe. Commanders could also grant short-term commissions to mid-career specialists in technology, logistics and finance. The US demonstrated this in 2025, when its Army Reserve commissioned executives from Meta, OpenAI and Palantir as lieutenant colonels, while its Navy Reserve recruited Wall Street bankers for financial warfare.

Critics will cite fiscal constraints and the risk of campus politicisation, warning that the elite will simply buy exemptions. The cost argument ignores the alternative, since a short course and a part-time reserve avoid the permanent payroll of a larger standing army. As for politicisation, that is a design problem. By ensuring that no exemptions are granted to anyone, including the children of generals, ministers and industrialists, national service ceases to be a factional tool and treats all citizens as equals.

These are extraordinary times. Had these proposals been voiced a few years ago, they would have been dismissed as alarmist paranoia. What 2026 has proven, however, is that the only remaining rule of the global order is that no rules apply. The paralysis of the United Nations, the routine defiance of the Geneva Conventions and the international community’s acceptance of war criminals like Benjamin Netanyahu signal the end of multilateral accountability. This lawless landscape leaves every nation to guard its own peace.

Peace belongs to the prepared, and a nation that stands ready gives its adversaries no cause to test it and its children no cause to fear. Pakistan must build that readiness now, while the lights still burn.

Syed Ali Shehryar The writer is a strategy consultant, a graduate of Pakistan’s National Security Workshop (NDU) and a Fulbright Scholar from New York University. He can be reached at shehryar@ nyu.edu.

Mesmerised by superficial displays of strength, Pakistani society has settled into a dangerous passivity, while its affluent classes have retreated into insular luxury. A casual walk through any Pakistani city reveals the rot: convoys of double-cabin trucks clearing the streets, carrying young men flashing weapons for digital clout. A society that mistakes privilege for power cannot absorb a blow from three sides. As history demonstrates, national resolve is forged long before a crisis arrives, built in the homes, schools and civic institutions that stand firm when geopolitical pressure finally hits.

Civil preparedness, therefore, becomes the vital first step. If war shuts the Persian Gulf, Pakistan’s markets will empty and its power grid will come under strain. Pakistan must respond by publishing household readiness guides, training neighbourhood volunteers in first aid and rescue, and issuing rationing guidelines for grain and fuel. At the national level, the time has come to scale up strategic reserves of essential commodities. A prepared citizenry prevents internal chaos, preserving the army’s focus on the front line.

Protecting the home also requires preparing the people inside it through mandatory national service. Pakistan has long maintained a rigid firewall between soldier and civilian, leaving the public to treat national defence as someone else’s responsibility. Compulsory training breaks this divide while formative habits are still taking shape. Finland backs a small peacetime army with male conscription, allowing commanders to mobilise hundreds of thousands of reservists within days, while Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan enforce national service and reserve obligations. Mandatory basic training for students would instil discipline, first-aid skills and a habit of service. A young Pakistani who serves alongside classmates from every class and province learns that the country belongs to all of them.

Training builds the citizen, while a reserve system keeps that citizen on call. A slow, isolated standing army cannot carry an asymmetric war alone, yet Pakistan offers recruits a multi-decade career or nothing. A reserve system would allow graduates who have served three to five years to pause their military careers and return when a crisis erupts, whether war or catastrophe. Commanders could also grant short-term commissions to mid-career specialists in technology, logistics and finance. The US demonstrated this in 2025, when its Army Reserve commissioned executives from Meta, OpenAI and Palantir as lieutenant colonels, while its Navy Reserve recruited Wall Street bankers for financial warfare.

Critics will cite fiscal constraints and the risk of campus politicisation, warning that the elite will simply buy exemptions. The cost argument ignores the alternative, since a short course and a part-time reserve avoid the permanent payroll of a larger standing army. As for politicisation, that is a design problem. By ensuring that no exemptions are granted to anyone, including the children of generals, ministers and industrialists, national

service ceases to be a factional tool and treats all citizens as equals.

These are extraordinary times. Had these proposals been voiced a few years ago, they would have been dismissed as alarmist paranoia. What 2026 has proven, however, is that the only remaining rule of the global order is that no rules apply. The paralysis of the United Nations, the routine defiance of the Geneva Conventions and the international community’s acceptance of war criminals like Benjamin Netanyahu signal the end of multilateral accountability. This lawless landscape leaves every nation to guard its own peace.

Peace belongs to the prepared, and a nation that stands ready gives its adversaries no cause to test it and its children no cause to fear. Pakistan must build that readiness now, while the lights still burn.

Syed Ali Shehryar

headline: Darkest Day in Kashmir
description: Kashmiris on both sides of the Line of Control, in Pakistan and worldwide, observed Black Day on 27 October 2026, marking 79 years since Indian troops entered
author: Muhammad Zahid Raffat
article_text:
Kashmiris on both sides of the Line of Control, in Pakistan and worldwide, observed Black Day on 27 October 2026, marking 79 years since Indian troops entered Jammu and Kashmir in 1947. The occasion recalled an unresolved dispute, generations of suffering and the demand of the Kashmiri people for self-determination.

On 27 October 1947, Indian troops were airlifted into Kashmir following Maharaja Hari Singh’s controversial accession to India. The decision, taken without consulting the population, became the foundation of a conflict that continues to threaten regional peace. Subsequent United Nations Security Council resolutions envisaged a plebiscite to determine the territory’s future, but that commitment remains unfulfilled.

The central question is unchanged: why should millions of Kashmiris be denied the opportunity to determine their political future? An instrument signed by a ruler cannot permanently substitute for the aspirations of his people. No settlement can command lasting legitimacy without their consent.

In messages marking Black Day, Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership reaffirmed the country’s moral, diplomatic and political support for Kashmiris and called for a peaceful settlement consistent with UN resolutions. Their statements also drew attention to continuing allegations of human rights violations, restrictions and political repression in Indian-administered Kashmir.

Pakistan has consistently maintained that Kashmir is more than a territorial disagreement between neighbouring states. It concerns the fundamental rights and political future of millions. The right to self-determination cannot be indefinitely postponed because its exercise is inconvenient for a powerful government.

Generations of Kashmiris have grown up amid conflict, uncertainty and restrictions on political freedoms. Families have lost loved ones, while others have endured displacement and prolonged insecurity. Yet their demand for dignity and political representation has persisted. Their suffering deserves sustained international scrutiny, not occasional statements of concern.

That failure was especially striking as the United Nations observed its founding anniversary on 24 October, three days before Kashmir Black Day. The occasion celebrated achievements in peace and international cooperation, but it should also have prompted reflection on unresolved commitments. Kashmir remains a glaring test of the organisation’s ability to uphold the principles on which it was founded.

The question is not simply whether international institutions possess the means to advance a settlement, but whether influential governments have the political will. History shows that global powers can act decisively when their strategic interests demand it. When economic partnerships and geopolitical calculations intervene, however, appeals to international law often lose their urgency.

India’s economic and diplomatic influence has made many governments reluctant to challenge its Kashmir policies. This is particularly disappointing when countries that champion democracy, civil liberties and the rule of law appear unwilling to apply those principles consistently. Human rights should not become secondary considerations because a state is an important commercial or strategic partner.

India’s claim to democratic leadership must also be judged against its treatment of Kashmiris. Democracy requires more than elections; it demands the protection of freedoms, meaningful political participation and respect for those governed. Restrictions on political expression and concerns about human rights undermine confidence in any claim that the dispute has been satisfactorily resolved.

Changes to residency and domicile rules have also generated fears that the territory’s demographic and political character could be altered. Such concerns cannot be dismissed. Policies perceived as weakening the local population’s influence only deepen mistrust and make reconciliation more difficult.

For Pakistan, Kashmir remains the unfinished agenda of partition, connected to the country through geography, history, culture and religion. Pakistan’s longstanding diplomatic support is therefore significant, but solidarity must be matched by persistent, purposeful engagement. Raising the issue at international forums matters; building wider support for a credible political process matters even more.

A peaceful resolution is essential to stability across South Asia. Two nuclear-armed neighbours cannot afford to leave such a profound disagreement indefinitely exposed to fresh crises. Dialogue, respect for international obligations and recognition of Kashmiri aspirations must form the basis of a durable settlement.

The international community, meanwhile, must recognise that silence is not neutrality when fundamental rights are at stake. Governments and human rights organisations should continue to scrutinise abuses, seek accountability and encourage negotiations without allowing strategic convenience to determine whose suffering merits attention.

Black Day was not merely a remembrance of events in 1947. It was a reminder that 79 years have passed without a settlement capable of meeting the aspirations of the Kashmiri people. Commemorations are important, but they must lead to sustained action rather than another cycle of statements followed by silence.

Pakistan should continue to support the Kashmiri people through peaceful diplomatic means and press for a resolution that allows them a genuine voice in their future. Justice delayed across generations cannot be treated as an acceptable permanent arrangement. The international community must turn its professed principles into meaningful engagement so that Kashmiris may finally live with dignity, security and freedom.

Muhammad Zahid Rifat The writer is Lahore-based Freelance Journalist, Columnist and retired Deputy Controller (News), Radio Pakistan, Islamabad and can be reached at zahidriffat@gmail.com

article_text:
At a time when the Middle Eastern crisis stands on the precipice of a second round, with both Washington and Tel Aviv gathering forces and replenishing their munitions, an American consortium’s proposal to invest $4.4 billion in Pakistan’s LNG infrastructure comes as something of a surprise. This hardly seems the most opportune moment to enter the fossil fuel business in the shadow of the Strait of Hormuz, particularly when another regional conflagration could send energy markets into turmoil.

Here, Pakistan has learnt through its long and chequered history of dealing with Washington, the American apple seldom arrives without some poison.

The proposed investment, backed by the Trump administration, envisages LNG storage facilities at Port Qasim and a 1,100km pipeline transporting gas upcountry. On paper, it offers much-needed infrastructure and an opportunity to strengthen Pakistan’s energy security. But the timing, scale and political sponsorship of the proposal warrant considerable scrutiny.

Perhaps this is a diplomatic makeweight, intended to sway Islamabad at a particularly sensitive geopolitical juncture. Perhaps it is simply an opportunity for American energy interests to make money from the very instability their country’s foreign policy has helped create. President Trump has himself boasted of the billions flowing into American oil interests amid the Middle Eastern conflict.

Either way, Pakistan must recognise the dangers of exchanging one energy dependency for another. Europe’s experience with the Nord Stream sabotage, an enormous energy crisis, and now a heavy dependency on the US, demonstrates how quickly commercial infrastructure can become a geopolitical liability.

American investment is not inherently unwelcome, but neither is it inherently benign. Islamabad must approach this offer with its eyes open, remembering that the American energy lobby has long been intertwined with Washington’s military and geopolitical ambitions.

It is, after all, one of the original war lobbies.

headline: Some Relief
description: The government knew that no matter how many adjustments it made to energy policies, supply chains or petroleum levies, sooner or later it would have to absorb
author: The Nation
article_text:
The government knew that no matter how many adjustments it made to energy policies, supply chains or petroleum levies, sooner or later it would have to absorb some financial pain to keep fuel within reach of ordinary Pakistanis. With the Middle East crisis far from settled and international prices remaining dangerously elevated, that moment has arrived.

The decision to have oil refineries absorb approximately Rs15 billion monthly, averting a Rs15-per-litre increase in petrol prices, is a welcome reprieve. Alongside the targeted fuel subsidy scheme, it offers some protection against the economic fallout of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

The relief is modest, especially for households already struggling with inflated living costs. Yet relief is relief, and even a small concession is preferable to passing the full burden on to consumers.

The larger question is how long such measures can last. Refineries cannot indefinitely shoulder rising costs, nor can the treasury remain immune if international prices climb further. Will the government deepen its intervention if the conflict intensifies? Can it continue protecting consumers without compromising supplies or public finances?

That such extraordinary measures are necessary confirms the seriousness of the global energy crunch. Ministers insist Pakistan has sufficient supplies for November, but securing fuel for the coming winter could prove more difficult.

The government deserves credit for cushioning the immediate blow, but must also strengthen reserves, diversify supply arrangements and prepare for worse.

For Pakistanis, the message is sobering: this reprieve is welcome, but the energy crisis is far from over, and difficult days may lie ahead.
